title: My two friends, why does love grow fresh again?
intro: Khalil Mardam places these ten verses among the poems Ali ibn al-Jahm wrote in prison. Layla finds her way past guards who scarcely sleep, and answers the prisoner in her own voice. The iron on his ankles draws from him first a joke meant to comfort her, then an expression of hope in the caliph.

translation: My two friends, why does love grow fresh again
with time, when days wear out all that is new?
1.sharh: He appeals to the traditional pair of travelling companions. Love grows newer by the very process that wears everything else away.

translation: Why do beautiful women’s promises earn reproach,
when no one may reproach Layla’s?
2.sharh: Behind the question lies the familiar accusation that beautiful women break their promises. Layla is the one woman he will hear no word against.

translation: She came as night let down its curtains,
while the prison guards took little sleep.
3.sharh: The curtain seems to promise the lovers a room of their own. The second half reveals where they really are and how little protection darkness affords.

translation: I said, “How did you dare come this way?
Even a breath of wind can scarcely get in.”
4.sharh: His first words are for the danger she ran. If the way constricts even the wind’s breath, her getting through is an extraordinary act of will.

translation: She said, “I held out, then did as longing bade.
The worst heart a lover can have is a stout one.”
5.sharh: She claims the visit as her choice. A quality usually admired, the strength to hold out, would have kept her away from the person she loves.

translation: She spoke her grief aloud. Her tears ran
down her cheek as her neck twined round mine.
6.sharh: She has finished justifying the visit and can finally give way to distress. The repeated Arabic word for neck brings their two bodies together.

translation: I told her, as tears ran their several ways
and longing fed the fire of love,
7.sharh: The sentence hangs on “I told her”. Before we hear his words, we see tears taking different paths and the same longing burning beneath them.

translation: “While the one you love is safe, they are alike,
the turns of fortune, easy and hard.
8.sharh: The man in chains offers comfort to his visitor. What looks like disaster loses its force once she sees that the person she came for is alive.

translation: Don’t be distressed at the sight of his fetters.
A man’s fetters are his anklets.
9.sharh: An anklet and a fetter circle the same part of the body. The prisoner makes that small resemblance carry a brave joke for Layla’s sake.

translation: Don’t be dismayed that my days of ease are gone.
The Commander of the Faithful will bring them back.”
10.sharh: The last assurance to Layla also serves as a discreet appeal. The caliph, named by his title, has the power to make the prediction come true.

1.1.1.head: خَليل
1.1.1.meaning: A close friend. The speaker addresses two.

1.1.5.head: جِدَّة
1.1.5.meaning: Freshness, the quality of being new.

2.1.3.head: غانِيَة
2.1.3.meaning: A beautiful woman whose gifts of nature suffice for adornment.

2.1.4.head: ذَميمَة
2.1.4.meaning: Blameworthy, here said of a promise held to be unreliable.

3.1.1.head: أَلَمَّ
3.1.1.meaning: Called on someone, paid a brief visit.

3.1.2.head: جُنح
3.1.2.meaning: A stretch of the night under gathering darkness.

4.2.1.head: حَرَّجَ
4.2.1.meaning: To hem in or restrict passage.

6.2.5.head: جيد
6.2.5.meaning: The neck, particularly when its grace is in view.

7.2.4.head: أَذكى
7.2.4.meaning: To kindle or feed a flame.

10.2.2-3.head: أَمير المُؤمِنين
10.2.2-3.meaning: Amir al-mu'minin, the caliph’s title, literally “Commander of the Faithful”.
